clues.title: Vibe: clean city-state, tall apartment blocks
text: Singapore is a highly developed city-state, characterised by an overall **cleanliness and orderliness**.
Main roads are often divided, and commonly feature black-and-white curbs and double yellow outside lines. You will often see tall apartment blocks nearby.
NOTE: In many cases, this “general look” is all you need to easily identify Singapore. Nevertheless, we have listed some more specific tips below.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A very clean, orderly city. Divided main roads, black-and-white curbs, double yellow lines at the edge, and tall apartment blocks nearby. Often enough on its own.

clues.title: Sign: green street name, rounded corners
text: All street name signs in Singapore follow this **unique format**. They are green, with rounded edges and a distinct white font.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Street name signs are green with rounded corners and a distinctive white font. This format is unique to the country.

clues.title: Plate: black with white text, not split
text: Most Singaporean licence plates are **black, with white text**. Occasionally, you will be able to see the British style **white-and-yellow** plates and very rarely red plates.
NOTE: Neighbouring Malaysia and Indonesia also use black plates with white text. However, the letters will usually be divided into two or three sections - this is not the case for Singaporean plates.

images.caption: Singaporean plates: front, rear, standard and offpeak

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most plates are black with white text. Older ones can be white-and-yellow, and red is very rare. Malaysia and Indonesia look alike, but their letters are split into sections.

differs.how: Letters are split into two or three sections
Letters are split into two or three sections

clues.title: Sign: green direction sign, 3-letter expressway
text: Directional signs are also **green**, with white letters and English writing.
NOTE: Expressways each have a **three-letter code** (e.g. TPE), making them easy to spot on signs.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Direction signs are green with white English text. Each expressway has a three-letter code, such as TPE, which makes them easy to spot.

clues.title: Sign: road signs on a white square
text: Road signs in Singapore are unique in that they are always set on a **square white background**.
NOTE: Road signs in almost all other countries will not have this square background.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Road signs sit on a square white background. Almost no other country does this.

clues.title: Plants: rain trees along main roads
text: **Rain trees** are seen all around Singapore, and are often planted along main roads.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Rain trees, wide trees with big spreading crowns, are common and often planted along main roads.

clues.title: Road markings: big warning words, HUMP AHEAD
text: Warnings are often written **on the road** in large letters, such as the famous “HUMP AHEAD”.

images.caption: Road surface with the words HUMP and AHEAD painted in big white letters

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Warnings are painted on the road in large letters, such as the well-known HUMP AHEAD.

clues.title: Vehicles: lime-green buses
text: Singaporean buses are mostly **lime-green**, making them easily recognisable. Other designs can also be found, for example the [white-and-purple SBS Transit variants](https://goo.gl/maps/SXeRNoTSsTqTmy5BA).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Buses are mostly lime green. Other colours exist too, like the white-and-purple SBS Transit buses.

clues.title: Bollard: concrete with black-yellow bands
text: Moreover, all bus stops are protected by **concrete bollards** with unique black-and-yellow **warning bands**.
NOTE: Similar, but not quite identical designs are found in some Malaysian cities.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bus stops are protected by concrete bollards with black-and-yellow warning bands. Some Malaysian cities have similar, but not identical, ones.

differs.how: Similar bollards in some cities, but the design is not identical

clues.title: Road markings: yellow bus-leaving box with arrow
text: In addition to the concrete bollards on bus stops, Singapore sometimes has a unique and yellow **bus-leaving box** with an **arrow** on the street.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Besides the bollards, bus stops sometimes have a yellow box painted on the road with an arrow, where buses pull out.

clues.title: Traffic lights: curved metal sheet with holes
text: Almost all Singaporean traffic lights follow this design and are supported by a curved **sheet of metal** containing several **holes**.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Almost all traffic lights are backed by a curved sheet of metal with several holes in it.

clues.title: Sign: street named after the neighbourhood
text: Many streets are named after the neighbourhood they are in, especially in the suburbs.

NOTE: These neighbourhood names appear very quickly on the map, so you can save yourself a lot of time scanning for 5k’s that way. For example, the sign in the image refers to Street 31 in the neighbourhood of Ang Mo Kio.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Suburban streets are often named after their neighbourhood, e.g. Street 31 in Ang Mo Kio. That lets you find the area on the map quickly.

clues.title: Landscape: industrial area, cranes, containers
text: The Tuas planning area is an **industrial area** that is characterised by straight roads, industrial complexes, cranes and shipping containers, making it recognisable.

images.caption: Industrial area with cranes and containers beside the road

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A western industrial zone with straight roads, big factories, cranes and shipping containers.

clues.title: Area: resort island, green signs, winding roads
text: You can easily recognise the **island of Sentosa** thanks to the green signposts, winding roads and general resort feel. Occasionally you might see a green lane like [this](https://goo.gl/maps/hrc9MLAc4F6GQihy5) as well.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A resort island with green signposts, winding roads and a holiday feel. You may spot a green lane marking too.

clues.title: Google car: Gen 3 walker, forest and camo hat
text: The Generation 3 **trekker on Pulau Ubin** can be identified by the unusually rural forest coverage and the camouflage-type hat sometimes visible when looking down.

images.caption: Red circle at top left zooms in on the walker's camouflage-patterned hat

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A Gen 3 backpack camera on a rural, forested island. Looking down, you may see the walker's camouflage-style hat.

clues.title: Google car: Gen 3 walker, smooth roads, sea
text: You can recognise **St John and Lazarus Islands** thanks to the Generation 3 trekker, the smooth asphalt roads and the sea almost always nearby.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Two small islands filmed on foot with the Gen 3 camera. Smooth asphalt roads, and the sea is almost always close.

clues.title: Paths: red paving stones everywhere
text: The miniscule Kusu Island is easily identifiable because of the **red paving stones** used for the entire pathway.

images.caption: A paved footpath made of red paving stones

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A tiny island where the whole walkway is paved with red stones.

clues.title: Sign: stop sign with white square outline
text: The edge of the stop signs in Singapore has a white square outline making it unique.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Stop signs have a white square outline around the red shape, which makes them unique.
